Title:
[Bug]: InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

- Hi @username_0, thanks for your report. Node.js' internal thread pool has a default size of 4 and is used for both I/O and mining. Please try to increase the number of threads by setting the environment variable `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (e.g. `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node index.js ...`) and see if the problem persists.

<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output. Normal internal logs are logged to stderr and can be switched on using the `RUST_LOG` environment variable. ```text ---------------------------------------------------------- Bringing up virtual network consisting of a seed node, 15 nodes and 2 wallets ---------------------------------------------------------- Node 'Bob' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' Node 'Carol' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' Node 'Charlie' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' (snip...) ---------------------------------------------------------- Discovery is done. ---------------------------------------------------------- ⚡️🎉😎 'Vanna' discovered peer 'Plod (7bb7b1d55953e391)' ([7bb7b1d55953e391] PK=88aed2306b39d4c4659b6a41d98199c5a8acb48155ba1e2fa6c356edece7c251 Features=NONE | COMMUNICATION_CLIENT) in 11014ms (snip...) ``` ## How Has This Been Tested? <!--- Please describe in detail how you tested your changes. --> <!--- Include details of your testing environment, and the tests you ran to --> <!--- see how your change affects other areas of the code, etc. --> _memorynet_ is a test of these changes. ## Types of changes <!--- What types of changes does your code introduce? Put an `x` in all the boxes that apply: --> * [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) * [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) * [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change) * [x] Feature refactor (No new feature or functional changes, but performance or technical debt improvements) * [x] New Tests * [ ] Documentation ## Checklist: <!--- Go over all the following points, and put an `x` in all the boxes that apply. --> * [x] I'm merging against the `development` branch. * [x] I ran `cargo-fmt --all` before pushing. * [x] I have squashed my commits into a single commit. * [ ] My change requires a change to the documentation. * [ ] I have updated the documentation accordingly. * [x] I have added tests to cover my changes.

Title:
[Bug]: InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

- @username_2 Hi Vince, So the point I was trying to make (badly!!) above was that something strange was going on to cause a change in the name of the network interface between the time Packer/VMware built the box and Vagrant/VMware ran it. To the best of my knowledge Vagrant doesn't actually do very much at all with regard to setting up the _default_ network interface. Instead it just expects, and in fact _requires_, the network interface to be correctly configured. In other words the configuration of the interface is done when the box is built, _not_ when it is run with Vagrant. It is the guest itself that determines the name for the network interface - not Vagrant. It used to be the case that network device names were arbitrarily assigned on first boot and then persisted through the use of a udev script. More recently this practice has changed and network interface names are now _determined_ through the use of a tool called [biosdevname](https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-US/Red_Hat_Enterprise_Linux/7/html/Networking_Guide/sec-Consistent_Network_Device_Naming_Using_biosdevname.html). Essentially biosdevname uses the location of the network device (as reported by the system BIOS) to set the device name. So, for example, a dual port network card installed in PCI slot 1 on the motherboard will result in the two interfaces named p1p1 and p1p2 respectively - see the link to the Red Hat doc for (better!) details. Clearly, virtual machines don't have physical slots or physical cards and instead everything is emulated. The 'physical' location of devices on the virtual motherboard are then specified within a configuration file. For Virtualbox this is an XML file with the .vbox extension; VMware stores it's settings in a .vmx file. When a Vagrant box is built this file is bundled into the .box file along with the VM's hard disk file and a few others. This file should, and at least for me _does_ include the physical location of the the network interface: `...` `ethernet0.pcislotnumber = "33"` `...` Essentially my box was built with its network card located in PCI slot **33**. This results in a network interface of name **ens33** and corresponding network configuration script at /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-**ens33**. When the box is run with Vagrant the required files for the new VM are copied, imported, and created as required. Unfortunately, the setting specifying what PCI slot the network interface was plugged into is _not_ preserved from the original .vmx file bundled with the box. From my _Vagrant_ machines .vmx file: `...` `ethernet0.pciSlotNumber = "32"` `...` This means my Vagrant VM now has a network interface named **ens32**. The configuration scripts within the VM (/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-ens33) are not run since the interface clearly doesn't exist. The error we've all seen is the network.service complaining about the fact that this interface is _configured_ - there _is_ an ifcfg-ens33 file - but it is missing from the system. Since the ens32 interface has no corresponding configuration script nothing happens with it and networking for our VM fails! Since I create my own boxes, I have been able to get around this problem (**and fix the errors seen**) by explicitly setting the location the PCI slot the network card uses in both the Packer build configuration file and the Vagrantfile _bundled_ inside the created box. Explicitly setting this within the _user_ configured or _VM specific_ Vagrantfile should work as well. For VMware the relevant setting can be explicitly defined by setting: `...` ` # VMware provider specific options` ` config.vm.provider 'vmware_fusion' do |vf|` ` vf.vmx['ethernet0.pcislotnumber'] = '33' ` end` `...` I believe settings for Virtualbox can be configured in a similar way. Of course you do need to know the _original_ setting the box was built with but since Vagrant boxes are essentially just tar archives you should be able to untar the box and take a peek at the .vbox or .vmx file to see what the setting should be! This could be used as a possible workaround until this is fixed... @username_3 All told, _if_ (!!) I've got all this right then this issue should really be solved by Vagrant reading and using the network card location from the .vbox or .vmx file bundled with the box. This would ensure the network device name is the same as when the box was created and should resolve this issue. Of course, I could have all this wrong and the root cause of the issue may be something else entirely :). However, I can say that what I've done has worked for me... Hope that helps. Dan

Unfortunately I can't figure out how you set the PCI slot to use for the NIC card with Virtualbox... **The workaround does not work so well for boxes with multiple virtual NICs** - it looks like Vagrant expects the default NIC it uses to communicate with the VM to be in slot 32! With a multi NIC VM it looks as though Vagrant blows away the default ifcfg-ens33 with what should be the second NICs network settings... Fixing the default NIC so it is located in PCI slot **32** in the Packer build configuration file and within the boxes bundled Vagrantfile works well enough and again fixes the issue - even for multi NIC Vagrant machines. I also think that #7514 is related or caused by the same core issue - although it should be noted that the root cause has nothing to do with setting the host name per se. As stated in previous comments, the error is seen when the network service is restarted. This is because the network service is in a failed state. As such any script restarting the network service will fail (with set -e). ``` ==> default: Setting hostname... The following SSH command responded with a non-zero exit status. ... blah ... Restarting network (via systemctl): [FAILED] ... blah ... Job for network.service failed because the control process exited with error code. See "systemctl status network.service" and "journalctl -xe" for details. ``` Running journalctl -xe shows us why the network.service is in a failed state: ``` Jul 20 22:00:58 bento-centos72.localdomain network[11799]: Bringing up interface ens33: Error: Connection activation failed: No suitable device found for this connection. Jul 20 22:00:58 bento-centos72.localdomain network[11799]: [FAILED] ... blah ... -- Subject: Unit network.service has failed ``` The ens33 device does not exist. Instead we have ens32. ``` # ls /sys/class/net ens32 lo ``` When the Vagrant box was built the Ethernet device was located in PCI slot 33. This can be seen in the .vmx file bundled with the box. Now we are running the box with Vagrant the Ethernet device is in PCI slot 32. Again this can be seen in the .vmx file under the .vagrant directory or from debug output. Clearly this means that biosdevname will change the name of the network interface. The ifcfg-ens33 network-script intended to configure the network when the box is brought up is never run since the device is now missing. The end result of all this is the failed network.service. Again, I've gotten around this issue with my own CentOS boxes by explicitly setting the PCI slot for the network card to 32 (via vmx settings) both in Packers .json file and in the Vagrantfile bundled with the box. For the bento/centos-7.2 box in question, the issue can be reproduced and worked around with the following Vagrantfile: ``` ruby #-*- mode: ruby -*- # vi: set ft=ruby : Vagrant.configure(2) do |config| # Box config.vm.box = 'bento/centos-7.2' # Configure the guests hostname config.vm.hostname = 'bento-centos72.localdomain' # VMware Fusion specific workaround for #7533 and #7514 # Commenting this section out will reproduce the errors config.vm.provider 'vmware_fusion' do |vf| vf.vmx['ethernet0.pcislotnumber'] = '33' end end ``` Obviously this is a workaround and not a fix... So no idea if it properly bound on the correct network interfaces. Though it responds correctly on the `eth0` interface to other clients. So mdns advertising seems fine. Both of them seem to send malformed dns packets (which is fine, the error is caught properly and only printed to the log for informational purposes). `192.168.1.205` seems to send packets which are completely weird and `192.168.1.236` seems to be using non standardized (or experimental or deprecated) way of encoding label names. --- @username_8 thanks for your detailed work. Is there any particular reason why you manually defined the network interface for mdns? As you manually override the mechanism, interface detection seems fine and it also seems like ciao is normally advertising as it should. You said your switch (or whatever) does multicast forwarding. Does it block regular unicast traffic (or any other blocking)? Cause mdns may also send it's response via unicast (via udp) directly to the requesting client (if the client wishes to do so) [this is one of the thins bonjour-hap completely ignored]. Do you mind sharing what device `<IoTdeviceIP>` is? Seems to be a legacy unicast, one-shot querier. Reading your explanation it seems like the issue is happening in both broadcast domains right? And the time frames also seem pretty short. For a quick background info, a typical mdns advertising has a time-to-live of 4500 seconds, meaning 75 minutes. So if the announcement went through (and it does, as it appears in the discovery app at first), I would assume that I would stay there for at least 75 minutes. This means that the device decided by itself that it removes the advertising before the ttl ran out. This can happen for example when it's own queries don't get answered, or when it observes queries sent via multicast (without the unicast response flag) get not answered. I think the reason why 1.1.6 worked is because the old `bonjour-hap` pretty much spammed the whole network with hundreds of response packets, thus keeping the advertisement valid at all times. --- @username_32 Do i understand correctly: you can fully control your switches and devices via the Home App right? Only the automations on the Home Hub don't run? Could you check if you can fully operate the switches ON your Home Hub (meaning via Siri on Apple TV or Home Hub). I myself already experienced the issue that the automations didn't seem to be setup correctly. What helped me was, to just go into the automation Tab in the Home App, open the automation and click done so the automation gets saved again. Maybe that helps, maybe the issue is somewhere else, depending on the success of the steps above.

- @username_30 @username_34 you both saw the error which started like `received malformed packet from ...`, right (and you are probably still)? The error does not affect anything (only the device with the ip shown won't be able to receive the mdns advertisement, but that shouldn't be a big deal). As you said the mentioned IP address is assigned to some of your ubiquiti equipment right? I just pushed a minor update to the underlying mdns library which adjusts the error message shown in such a scenario to also include the data of the received packet. As Ubiquiti seems to not follow the standardized implementation for dns packets, it would want to have a look at the exact packet structure, to manually decode the packet and maybe raise an issue with them. So to update the underlying library, all you have to do is reinstall homebridge (by just running the regular install command like `sudo npm install -g homebridge`). As this isn't a major change I decided to not push a new homebridge update for that. Would be great if you could provide DEBUG logs with the updated error message. This update does not have any different changes besides the update error message.

- Hi @username_30 In general: This issue is NOT related to Unifi Networking. Your issue was forced by configuring VLANs... this is different. If you want to use multicast over VLANs you have to use a mDNS reflector, not a mDNS repeater. If you are using a UniFi Dream Machine it is not possible right now (not official supported, only on USG via JSON.config). Another thing: If you are using Philips Hue: it does not support connectivity over VLANs! The bridge may crash every few minutes and you will get a "not responding situation" if a mDNS packet is coming from an iOS device from a different VLAN / network. Workaround: You can setup homebridge in the same VLAN like your iOS devices. Connect your homebridge to the Philips Hue Bridge via a plugin. This is fully supported and will work great... and the mDNS packets are "flat" within the main network. But back to the roots: The described infrastructure is running in my home since over a year without any issues AND on UniFi without any problems. I have not made any infrastructure changes at the same time... and I am facing the issue since a few weeks. Please do not mix that.

- There is another thing, Multicast forwarding must ensure that TTL of packet does not get touched. Bonjour packets come with TTL of 1, this means that the moment they get routed, they become invalid. I have set my multicast forwarding to ensure that TTL does not get touched. - @username_8 actually the RFC defines a TTL of 255 🤔 https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6762#section-11 (Though the rfc references that old queries implementing previous draft would reject ip packets with less than 255 ttl)
- If you look a bit closer, their language is cautious. It says SHOULD in all caps, not MUST. It is not required, but SHOULD be used, unless you wish to restrict the limit of how many routing interfaces a multicast packet should go through before dying. Apple uses bonjour TTL of 1.

- To give some insights. We are currently preparing some other changes to improve stability of the HomeKit server. When we opened this issue to track issues with the migration from the `bonjour-hap` library (used in version `<= 1.1.6`) to the newly written `ciao` library (used with version `>=1.2.0`), we discovered that many people are experiencing the same symptoms (accessories with 'No response') though caused by totally different problems (It may also didn't help that we released 1.2.x at the same time as iOS 14 lol). With the .1, .2 and .3 released we could already squash some problems, which most people experienced here. To help us discover the problems faster and also to help the users having a much more reliable homebridge experience we are reworking some of the fundamental connection and plugin management. The thing is, this takes time. No one here is getting paid for working on homebridge or it's subsequent libraries. It's done in our free time and we are doing our best. We have the impression that most people are running fine with 1.2.x, though as we haven't any analytical data we can't exactly calculate how many people are actually running 1.2.x. And as there are also enough people having problems and as we currently haven't the capacity and time to process all issues posted here, we decided to revert the latest version of homebridge back to 1.1.6. So what to do now: * If you were running fine with 1.1.6 and had problems after upgrading to 1.2.x: downgrade back to 1.1.6 by reinstalling homebridge (NO NEED to RESET homebridge!) by running `sudo npm install -g homebridge` * If you are running 1.2.x (best case 1.2.3) and you have no problems: Everything fine, nothing to do. * If you are running 1.2.0, 1.2.1, 1.2.2 and have problems: You got two options, you can check if 1.2.3 is maybe working for you (`sudo npm install -g homebridge@1.2.3`) or you simply revert back to 1.1.6 as shown above. * If you have problems with 1.2.x AND 1.1.6 your issue is not caused by the service advertisement and currently out of the scope of this issue. You may want to check if any plugins are causing issues. If you uncovered any particular bug or can provide detailed information you are welcome to raise an issue with us. If someone wants to follow along the current development progress and process you can visit https://github.com/homebridge/HAP-NodeJS/projects/4 (the different columns are explained [here](https://github.com/homebridge/HAP-NodeJS/wiki/Release-Cycle#github-projects)). If you want to try the latest (publicly available) state of this planned release you can install the beta by running `sudo npm install -g homebridge@beta`.

- @username_46 This is actually caused by your plugin https://github.com/username_46/homebridge-denon-tv/blob/93af07281d6d6dcf2d2abcbec550ecbe571057aa/index.js#L307. `setCharacteristic` expects the characteristic to set as the first argument (exactly as you have done it `Characteristic.InputSourceType`) and the second value must be the new value, where you supply `Characteristic.InputSourceType` again, which is a function (or rather a constructor). Previous hap-nodejs version just gave up at this point when it couldn't convert the value to a valid value and took whatever it got. Latest beta will complain when it receives a function which is totally not a number and it can't easily convert it.

- @username_58 you are talking about `[Ozone] characteristic was supplied illegal value: number 303 exceeded maximum of 255. Supplying illegal values will throw errors in the future!`? This is caused by whatever plugin creates the `Ozone` accessory. HAP-NodeJS will correct the supplied value to the maximum allowed for the given characteristic (in this case 255). New version will now start notifying people so plugin owners can start fixing their stuff. Before we announce public beta testing we will still ask plugin owners (at least those who are signed up on our discord) to check their plugins. Long story short: nothing to worry about.

Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output. Normal internal logs are logged to stderr and can be switched on using the `RUST_LOG` environment variable. ```text ---------------------------------------------------------- Bringing up virtual network consisting of a seed node, 15 nodes and 2 wallets ---------------------------------------------------------- Node 'Bob' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' Node 'Carol' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' Node 'Charlie' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' (snip...) ---------------------------------------------------------- Discovery is done. ---------------------------------------------------------- ⚡️🎉😎 'Vanna' discovered peer 'Plod (7bb7b1d55953e391)' ([7bb7b1d55953e391] PK=88aed2306b39d4c4659b6a41d98199c5a8acb48155ba1e2fa6c356edece7c251 Features=NONE | COMMUNICATION_CLIENT) in 11014ms (snip...) ``` ## How Has This Been Tested? <!--- Please describe in detail how you tested your changes. --> <!--- Include details of your testing environment, and the tests you ran to --> <!--- see how your change affects other areas of the code, etc. --> _memorynet_ is a test of these changes. ## Types of changes <!--- What types of changes does your code introduce? Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

Summary:

Description:
h3. Summary +As a+ system admin on Windows +I want to+ be able to set network interface parameter {{confluence.cluster.interface}} on a fixed way +So that I can+ not use the name generated by Java and use one that is fixed on Windows instead h3. Problem Definition Customers report that the network interface name (for example, _eth0_) changes by itself on Windows, sometimes, on reboot. That is not a consistent behavior and cannot be reproduced. In this case, it changed form _eth6_ to _eth7_ and caused Synchrony to fail due to Hazelcast not finding it: {code} Hazelcast CANNOT start on this node. No matching network interface found.\nInterface matching must be either disabled or updated in the hazelcast.xml config file. {code} More information: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58632235/get-name-of-a-specific-network-interface-in-java http://hg.openjdk.java.net/jdk8/jdk8/jdk/file/82b276590b85/src/windows/native/java/net/NetworkInterface.c#l172 {quote} * Windows does not have any standard for device names so we are forced * to use our own convention which is based on the normal Unix naming * convention ("lo" for the loopback, eth0, eth1, .. for ethernet devices, * tr0, tr1, .. for token ring, and so on). This convention gives us * consistency across multiple Windows editions and also consistency with * Solaris/Linux device names. Note that we always enumerate in index * order and this ensures consistent device number across invocations. */ {quote} h3. Workaround Use the instruction on this kb, whenever that behavior is observed: [Hazelcast CANNOT start on this node. Title:
Improve robustness of integration tests that commonly have false positives

Description:
Why: The tests below are a hotbed for false positives due to a lack of assertions about the final state. What: Each of the tests now have checks to verify various quantities to ensure the final output is what we're expecting. To avoid making the tests more brittle I have avoided testing details that would be too specific.

Comments:

- Java doesn't have a permgen, that was a concept in 7 but was taken out in 8.
- OK, I've found the exact details [here](https://blogs.oracle.com/poonam/entry/about_g1_garbage_collector_permanent): `PermSpace` has been replaced by `Metaspace`, which by default is limited by the available memory. This still seems like a possible explanation for why the integration tests trigger OOM errors when run on a PC with "only" 6 GB of RAM. So my next step would be proving/disproving it.
- Does it actually use 6 gig? We restrict nodes to max 200mb of RAM by default, which is rather arbitrary and may not be appropriate (it was picked based on what an idle node needed when not under pressure to unblock people who think a Raspberry Pi is a sensible platform to run a node on ... like our CTO ;)) Check CordaCaplet to see the gory details.

Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output. Normal internal logs are logged to stderr and can be switched on using the `RUST_LOG` environment variable. ```text ---------------------------------------------------------- Bringing up virtual network consisting of a seed node, 15 nodes and 2 wallets ---------------------------------------------------------- Node 'Bob' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' Node 'Carol' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' Node 'Charlie' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' (snip...) ---------------------------------------------------------- Discovery is done. ---------------------------------------------------------- ⚡️🎉😎 'Vanna' discovered peer 'Plod (7bb7b1d55953e391)' ([7bb7b1d55953e391] PK=88aed2306b39d4c4659b6a41d98199c5a8acb48155ba1e2fa6c356edece7c251 Features=NONE | COMMUNICATION_CLIENT) in 11014ms (snip...) ``` ## How Has This Been Tested? <!--- Please describe in detail how you tested your changes. --> <!--- Include details of your testing environment, and the tests you ran to --> <!--- see how your change affects other areas of the code, etc. --> _memorynet_ is a test of these changes. ## Types of changes <!--- What types of changes does your code introduce? Put an `x` in all the boxes that apply: --> * [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) * [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) * [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change) * [x] Feature refactor (No new feature or functional changes, but performance or technical debt improvements) * [x] New Tests * [ ] Documentation ## Checklist: <!--- Go over all the following points, and put an `x` in all the boxes that apply. --> * [x] I'm merging against the `development` branch. * [x] I ran `cargo-fmt --all` before pushing. * [x] I have squashed my commits into a single commit. * [ ] My change requires a change to the documentation. * [ ] I have updated the documentation accordingly. * [x] I have added tests to cover my changes.

Comments:
- @username_0 can you share your configs from both clients? (Please redact the public & private keys, as well as the discovery key.)
- I've managed to get the right `Connection to ...` outputs on both sides, copy and pasted the PeerIDs on both sides and that seems to have solved the initial problem, but, I still can't ping from either device.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

Description:
h3. Summary +As a+ system admin on Windows +I want to+ be able to set network interface parameter {{confluence.cluster.interface}} on a fixed way +So that I can+ not use the name generated by Java and use one that is fixed on Windows instead h3. This convention gives us * consistency across multiple Windows editions and also consistency with * Solaris/Linux device names. Note that we always enumerate in index * order and this ensures consistent device number across invocations. */ {quote} h3. Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Title:
[Bug]: InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

Description:
h3. Summary +As a+ system admin on Windows +I want to+ be able to set network interface parameter {{confluence.cluster.interface}} on a fixed way +So that I can+ not use the name generated by Java and use one that is fixed on Windows instead h3. That is not a consistent behavior and cannot be reproduced. This convention gives us * consistency across multiple Windows editions and also consistency with * Solaris/Linux device names. Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output. Normal internal logs are logged to stderr and can be switched on using the `RUST_LOG` environment variable. ```text ---------------------------------------------------------- Bringing up virtual network consisting of a seed node, 15 nodes and 2 wallets ---------------------------------------------------------- Node 'Bob' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' Node 'Carol' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' Node 'Charlie' is joining the network via the seed node 'Alice' EVENT: 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' connected to 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' EVENT: 'Alice (1dc460f5fe4e3675)' got inbound connection from 'Charlie (d4eaac42550edbd9)' EVENT: 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' connected to 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' EVENT: 'Carol (dea46505688b5ac7)' got inbound connection from 'Bob (1d79bcc44d814748)' (snip...) ---------------------------------------------------------- Discovery is done. ---------------------------------------------------------- ⚡️🎉😎 'Vanna' discovered peer 'Plod (7bb7b1d55953e391)' ([7bb7b1d55953e391] PK=88aed2306b39d4c4659b6a41d98199c5a8acb48155ba1e2fa6c356edece7c251 Features=NONE | COMMUNICATION_CLIENT) in 11014ms (snip...) ``` ## How Has This Been Tested? <!--- Please describe in detail how you tested your changes. --> <!--- Include details of your testing environment, and the tests you ran to --> <!--- see how your change affects other areas of the code, etc. --> _memorynet_ is a test of these changes. ## Types of changes <!--- What types of changes does your code introduce? Put an `x` in all the boxes that apply: --> * [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) * [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) * [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change) * [x] Feature refactor (No new feature or functional changes, but performance or technical debt improvements) * [x] New Tests * [ ] Documentation ## Checklist: <!--- Go over all the following points, and put an `x` in all the boxes that apply. --> * [x] I'm merging against the `development` branch. * [x] I ran `cargo-fmt --all` before pushing. * [x] I have squashed my commits into a single commit. * [ ] My change requires a change to the documentation. * [ ] I have updated the documentation accordingly. * [x] I have added tests to cover my changes.

Title:
[Bug]: InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output. Title:
[Bug]: InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index.

Description:
### Welcome to Amazon SSP EKS Accelerator! - [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-eks-accelerator-for-terraform/issues) and didn't find any. ### Amazon EKS Accelerator Release version 1.21 ### What is your environment, configuration and the example used? ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } ``` ### What did you do and What did you see instead? Try to use bottlerocket ARM managed node group ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.6.0" } kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes" version = ">= 2.8.0" } helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm" version = ">= 2.4.1" } } backend "local" { path = "local_tf_state/terraform-main.tfstate" } } data "aws_region" "current" {} data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {} data "aws_eks_cluster" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "cluster" { name = module.eks-ssp.eks_cluster_id } provider "aws" { profile = "cluster-sandbox" region = "us-west-2" } [Truncated] ```shell The first managed node work group works, but the custom one with launch template got errors: ╷ │ Error: error creating EKS Node Group (salesrise-sandbox-dev-eks:btl-arm20220323050436112600000006): InvalidRequestException: Each network interface requires a device index. │ { │ RespMetadata: { │ StatusCode: 400, │ RequestID: "eb560489-96f8-4663-86f3-6f96eea9c7a4" │ }, │ Message_: "Each network interface requires a device index." │ } │ │ with module.eks-ssp.module.aws_eks_managed_node_groups["bottlerocket_arm"].aws_eks_node_group.managed_ng, │ on .terraform/modules/eks-ssp/modules/aws-eks-managed-node-groups/main.tf line 1, in resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng": │ 1: resource "aws_eks_node_group" "managed_ng" { │ ``` ```

Comments:
- encountered same issue.
- And I found that it only failed when `create_launch_template = true`, if I removed `create_launch_template = true` or use `create_launch_template = false`, the managed group could created successful. I think there must be some bug in creating launch template.
- Thanks for reporting this issue. We have noticed this issue few days ago when `terraform-aws-provider` released a new version `4.6.0` which introduced a breaking change for launch templates. Workaround is to set the provider version to `4.5.0` in your examples. However this issue has PR has been fixed merged now. See this issue for more details https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/issues/23766/ ```hcl aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "4.5.0" } ``` Try again and let us know if you still hit the same issue
- Hello, just some clarification in case someone else (noob like me) stumbles upon the same issue. If your case is that your terraform script broke in a half-complete state due to the template thing, chances are you are going to follow @username_2 instructions above and then proceed to hit `terraform init -upgrade` and then `terraform apply` to pick up where you left off. Personally I kept receiving the same error, and the reason was due to the fact that since I already had a state that I was trying to continue from, Terraform would find the existing launch template (that had initially failed) and continue using that. The problem is that, that template had already a problematic index. So it was a no go. The solution is to either do `terraform destroy` and start from scratch (thus creating a new template in the process) **OR** going to your AWS console: EC2 > Launch Templates , find your template created by Terraform and delete it. Then proceed with `terraform apply`. Admittedly you will have messed with cloud resources our of Terraform scope but it's a minor thing and since Terraform is awesome it can detect it and proceed without issue (again by recreating the template with the correct index). Thanks guys for your support! :-)
- @username_3 I think the later option BUT using Terraform. You can update the node group by making `create_launch_template = false` and re enable it again. I haven't tried this myself but this should work
- @username_2 Thank you, it works.

Summary:
Allow other ways to use confluence.cluster.interface on Windows

Description:
h3. Summary +As a+ system admin on Windows +I want to+ be able to set network interface parameter {{confluence.cluster.interface}} on a fixed way +So that I can+ not use the name generated by Java and use one that is fixed on Windows instead h3. Problem Definition Customers report that the network interface name (for example, _eth0_) changes by itself on Windows, sometimes, on reboot. That is not a consistent behavior and cannot be reproduced. In this case, it changed form _eth6_ to _eth7_ and caused Synchrony to fail due to Hazelcast not finding it: {code} Hazelcast CANNOT start on this node. No matching network interface found.\nInterface matching must be either disabled or updated in the hazelcast.xml config file. {code} More information: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58632235/get-name-of-a-specific-network-interface-in-java http://hg.openjdk.java.net/jdk8/jdk8/jdk/file/82b276590b85/src/windows/native/java/net/NetworkInterface.c#l172 {quote} * Windows does not have any standard for device names so we are forced * to use our own convention which is based on the normal Unix naming * convention ("lo" for the loopback, eth0, eth1, .. for ethernet devices, * tr0, tr1, .. for token ring, and so on). This convention gives us * consistency across multiple Windows editions and also consistency with * Solaris/Linux device names. Note that we always enumerate in index * order and this ensures consistent device number across invocations. */ {quote} h3.
